GeoInv3D · field-data test · 30 September 2026

Karnataka Gravity Inversion with Terrain: Comparing Regularizations

The six regularization settings of the 28 September comparison, run again at full resolution on AWS EC2 with the ground surface in the mesh and a terrain correction added to the Bouguer anomaly. This report shows what the terrain changes, what it leaves as it was, and whether the conclusions of the flat-earth comparison still hold.

Area
70 × 70 km, easting 641–711 km, northing 1634–1704 km (UTM 43N, EPSG:32643)
Data
NGPM Bouguer anomaly at 1 km (5,040 points) plus a terrain correction computed from the DEM (2.67 g/cc, to 50 km); second-order trend surface removed
Terrain
Copernicus GLO-90 DEM, 381–1092 m in the area; stations on the ground
Mesh
1 km × 1 km × 250 m core, 10 km below the lowest ground; about 20 km padding at the sides: 84 × 84 × 50 = 352,800 cells, 335,518 below the ground
Runs
8 full-resolution inversions on AWS EC2 (ap-south-1, c5.4xlarge), 4.5–8.5 minutes each, $0.67 in total; a 16-run 2 km study run locally

Summary

  • The Bouguer anomaly had no terrain correction, and it matters on the ridges. Computed from the DEM, the correction is small over most of the area (median 0.11 mGal at the nodes) but reaches 6.7 mGal on the Sandur ridges and exceeds 1 mGal at 393 of 5,040 nodes, against a data error of 0.5 mGal. The ridges run along the north-western part of the NW–SE Bouguer high.
  • The depth of the main body does not change. Under the main Bouguer high the centroid moves by at most 0.3 km for four of the five compact settings (-0.8 km for αs = 0.1, whose body now reaches the density bound): 3.1 km for β = 0.5, 3.6 km for L1–L2, 5.4 km for β = 1 and 7.7 km for β = 1.5, measured below the ground.
  • The terrain changes the top kilometre. With the correction the model gains dense rock directly under the ridges: the density summed over the top kilometre changes by up to 0.15 g/cc·km there, and the dense belt becomes a continuous line along the ridge in the 1 km slice. This is where the banded iron formation crops out (3.4 g/cc in the rock samples).
  • The conclusions of the flat-earth comparison hold. All six runs fit the data about equally well (χ²/N 0.93–1.13); the vertically integrated density maps correlate at 0.85–0.97 pairwise and at 0.97–1.00 with their flat-earth counterparts; the regularization still sets the depth.
  • The coarse 2 km study still works for screening. For three values of β it predicts the full-resolution centroid of the main body to within 0.5 km.
  • Recommendation. Use the terrain and the terrain correction as the standard set-up: they cost one DEM and 8 instead of 5–6 minutes per run. They matter for anything shallow and for the joint inversion with the magnetic data; for the depth and shape of the deep bodies the recommendation of the earlier report is unchanged (αs = 1, depth weighting with β between 0.5 and 1, reported as a range).
  • Caveat. Gravity data alone do not determine depth, with or without terrain. The terrain correction uses a 90 m DEM and is interpolated between stations about 1.6 km apart, so terrain closer than about 100 m to a station is not accounted for.

1Terrain, data and the runs

1.1The terrain correction

The NGPM Bouguer anomaly is a simple Bouguer anomaly: the station table reproduces it as free-air anomaly minus an infinite slab of 2.67 g/cc, with no terrain term (the check of 29 September). A slab is wrong wherever the ground is not flat: hills above a station pull upwards, and valleys below it are rock the slab removed that is not there. Both lower the anomaly, so the terrain correction is positive and is added.

The correction was computed from the Copernicus GLO-90 DEM (90 m cells) at each of the 3,269 NGPM stations in and within 10 km of the area, with the reduction density of 2.67 g/cc, out to 50 km. The DEM is used at three resolutions around each station: its bilinear surface within about 0.5 km (integrated in polar coordinates, so that the step between a station and its neighbouring cells does not count as a slab), 90 m prisms to 4.7 km, 450 m cells to 22.5 km and 1.8 km cells beyond. The code (geoinv3d/methods/terrain.py) reproduces the analytic attraction of a ring-shaped plateau to within 3% in each zone. The station heights in the table agree with the DEM: DEM minus station +1.5 m on average, standard deviation 4.5 m.

At the 1,941 stations inside the area the correction has a median of 0.10 mGal, exceeds 0.5 mGal at 197 and 1 mGal at 77 stations, and reaches 6.7 mGal on the ridge tops near 1,000 m. On average 0.12 mGal comes from the terrain between 0.5 and 4.7 km, 0.06 from 4.7–22.5 km, 0.05 from within 0.5 km and 0.02 from beyond 22.5 km.

The inverted data are the NGPM grid, which was interpolated from these stations. The complete anomaly is the smooth quantity, so the stations' corrections were gridded the same way (thin-plate spline) and added to the grid at its 1 km nodes (Figure 1). After the second-order trend is removed, the anomaly that is inverted changes by −0.7 to +6.0 mGal: up along the two Sandur ridges, slightly down elsewhere because the trend absorbs the mean. At the main Bouguer high itself, south-east of the ridges, the change is +0.4 mGal.

1.2The ground in the mesh

The mesh follows the ground: cells whose centres lie above the DEM (averaged to 450 m) are air and are left out, which leaves 335,518 of 352,800 cells. The layers are 250 m thick instead of the 500 m of the earlier runs, so that the relief (387–1137 m in the mesh) is three steps rather than one; the core reaches 10 km below the lowest ground. Each datum is placed on the ground at its node, at the DEM's elevation (382–1071 m).

The ground of the mesh is a staircase, so a station at its true elevation can lie inside the top cell of its column, with part of that cell's rock above it. The pipeline now moves such stations to the top of their column: 1,900 of 5,040 stations were raised, by 72 m on average and at most 313 m (in steep valleys, where a 1 km cell spans several hundred metres of relief).

All depths in this report are measured below the ground of each column, not below sea level. In the mesh the ground is at 637 m at both the main Bouguer high and the north-western high.

1.3Data and runs

With the correction the Bouguer anomaly ranges from −94.5 to −43.1 mGal. After removing a least-squares second-order trend surface (−96.0 to −75.2 mGal), the residual anomaly ranges from −16.5 to +32.2 mGal (Figure 2). Every point has an error of 0.5 mGal, as before.

The six runs are the settings of the 28 September report; they share the mesh, the data and the errors:

Common settings, unchanged: density contrast bounded to −0.2 to +0.5 g/cc; β chosen automatically for χ² = N; at most 30 iterations and 30 IRLS iterations; αx = αy = αz = 1 as length scales. Li & Oldenburg depth weighting weights the model norm by (z + z₀)−β/2, where z is the depth below the nearest station and z₀ half the smallest cell (now 125 m). Two more runs, with β = 1, separate the effects in Section 2.

2What the terrain changes

Three things differ from the earlier runs: the layers are 250 m instead of 500 m, the ground is in the mesh, and the data carry the terrain correction. Four runs with the same regularization (αs = 1, β = 1) take these steps one at a time:

Run (αs = 1, β = 1)χ²/NRMS (mGal)CoreBelow the coreD50 kmMain high, half-max kmMain high, centroid kmNW high, centroid kmIntegrated density: correlation with the last row
Flat earth, 500 m layers (28 Sep report)0.960.4983%15%4.83.0–8.05.62.80.976
Flat earth, 250 m layers0.890.4785%12%4.93.0–8.05.62.90.982
Terrain in the mesh, no terrain correction0.980.4984%12%4.63.0–7.85.42.80.989
Terrain in the mesh and terrain correction0.930.4884%13%4.63.0–7.85.42.81.000

Depths below the ground of each column. The last column compares the vertically integrated density map of each run with that of the last row.

  • Thinner layers change almost nothing. On a flat earth, 250 m layers give a centroid of 5.6 km under the main high against 5.6 km with 500 m layers, and the same half-maximum range.
  • With the ground in the mesh the main body keeps its depth below the ground. Its centroid is 5.4 km below the ground against 5.6 km on the flat earth. The ground there is now at 637 m instead of zero, so in elevation the body is 0.9 km higher: the depth weighting counts depth from the stations, and the body follows them. The data fit is the same.
  • The terrain correction leaves the deep body where it is (centroid 5.4 km) and changes the top of the model. Figure 4 shows the density summed over the top kilometre below the ground: with the correction there is more dense rock along the two ridges, up to 0.15 g/cc·km more, and the dense belt of the 1 km slice (Figure 3, right) becomes a continuous line along the south-western ridge.
  • Why the correction goes to the top. It is a short-wavelength signal that follows the ridges, a few kilometres wide. A compact model can only fit it with sources close to the surface, and the depth weighting of the deep body is not affected.

The shallow dense rock is geologically reasonable: the ridges are banded iron formation, 3.38–3.40 g/cc in the two samples from the area, which the 2.67 g/cc of the Bouguer slab and of the terrain correction underestimates by 0.7 g/cc. The terrain correction does not remove this excess; it removes the error of treating the hills as a flat slab, and what is left is fitted as density contrast in the hills.

3The six settings with terrain

3.1Data fit

All six runs reach the target fit with nearly the same statistics as on the flat earth (last column). The residual maps (Figure 5) have the same character as before:

  • Original settings: patches of positive and negative misfit at places with steep gradients, up to 8.1 mGal.
  • L1–L2: a broad positive residual over the main high and the north-eastern belt: the model underestimates the amplitude of the main anomalies. Its χ²/N is 1.11.
  • β = 1.5: a positive residual over the main high as well, χ²/N 1.13: with the ridges' extra 7 mGal the deepest model has more difficulty fitting the short wavelengths. On the flat earth it fitted best (0.86).
  • β = 0.5, β = 1 and αs = 0.1: the least structured residuals, mostly short-wavelength stripes along strike and the isolated points near (660, 1680) and (702, 1659) km that appear in every model.

3.2Lateral structure

Figure 6 shows five models at about 2, 5 and 8 km below the mean ground. The top row of Figure 7 shows the vertically integrated density, the bottom row the centroid depth of each column.

  • The integrated density maps are nearly the same. Pairwise correlations are 0.85–0.97, and no less than 0.90 without the original settings. The NW–SE dense belt, the secondary high at its north-western end and the parallel low-density belts to the east have the same position and strike in every model.
  • They are also the maps of the flat-earth runs. Setting by setting, the integrated density with terrain correlates at 0.97–1.00 with the flat-earth result.
  • The centroid depth maps differ between settings as they did before: 2–4 km for β = 0.5 and L1–L2, 4–6 km for β = 1, 6–8 km and more for β = 1.5.

Figure 8 shows an E–W section through the main Bouguer high, and Figure 9 the distribution of |mass| with depth. The table gives where the mass lies and measures of the density profiles under the main Bouguer high (easting 671.5 km, northing 1664.5 km) and the north-western high (650.5, 1682.5 km). As before, depth is given as the centroid of the positive density contrast, because bodies held at the +0.5 g/cc bound have no single peak; the half-maximum range is measured between cell edges.

  • The original settings still give columns. Under the main high the density contrast is 0.17 g/cc from the surface to 16.0 km, the bottom of the mesh; 33% of the mass lies below the core and 38% in the lateral padding.
  • The other five have a base. The main body ends above 12 km, and at least 81% of the mass lies in the core (61% for β = 1.5).
  • β controls the depth monotonically. For β = 0.5, 1 and 1.5 the centroid of the main body is at 3.1, 5.4 and 7.7 km, the half-maximum range 1.5–4.5, 3.0–7.8 and 4.2–11.0 km.
  • L1–L2 stays close to β = 0.5: half-maximum range 1.8–4.8 km, centroids 0.5 km apart.
  • αs = 0.1 now behaves like αs = 1. Its main body reaches the bound (peak 0.50 g/cc) and its centroid is at 5.5 km, 0.2 km from the β = 1 run; on the flat earth it stayed just below the bound and 0.8 km deeper.
  • The north-western high is always shallower. Apart from the original settings, its centroid lies at 1.8–3.6 km, 1.3–4.1 km above that of the main high.

  • The five compact settings keep their depths. The centroid under the main high moves by −0.8 to +0.1 km; the ordering of the settings and the spread between them (from 3.1 to 7.7 km) are those of the flat-earth comparison.
  • The original settings change most, but only because their columns end where the mesh ends: this mesh reaches 15.3 km below sea level, the earlier one 21.4 km.
  • The differences between regularizations are far larger than the effect of the terrain. Changing β from 0.5 to 1.5 moves the centroid by 4.6 km; adding the terrain and its correction moves it by at most 0.3 km at a fixed setting with αs = 1.

"sensitivity" is SimPEG's sensitivity weighting, "β = …" Li & Oldenburg depth weighting. Red cells as in Section 3.3.

  • The trends are those of the flat-earth study. αs decides whether the model reaches the bottom of the mesh: with sensitivity weighting, αs = 10⁻⁴, 10⁻², 0.1 and 1 leave 34%, 30%, 18% and 15% of the mass below the core. Depth weighting decides the lateral leakage: 35% of the mass in the lateral padding with sensitivity weighting, 4%–10% with depth weighting.
  • β sets the mean depth: β = 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 give main-body centroids of 3.2, 5.2, 7.3 and 9.3 km.
  • Against the 1 km runs (Figure 12) the coarse centroid is within 0.5 km for the three values of β and within 0.5 km for αs = 0.1. The coarse mesh remains good for screening β; its 2 km cells cannot hold the shallow dense rock of the ridges.

5Recommendations

  • Make the terrain the default for field data. A DEM in the job (topography: {file}), stations on the ground, and the terrain correction added to simple Bouguer anomalies. The pipeline already reports whether a station table contains a terrain correction; the correction itself is now in geoinv3d/methods/terrain.py and is applied in the data preparation (karnataka_inputs/prepare_inputs.py).
  • Settings: unchanged. Sparse, αs = 1, p = [0,2,2,2], Li & Oldenburg depth weighting with β between 0.5 and 1, reported as a depth range (main-body centroid 3.1–5.4 km below the ground), with L1–L2 as an independent check.
  • Interpret the top kilometre only with the terrain correction. Without it the ridges' signal is missing from the data, and the shallow dense rock along them is underestimated.
  • A better terrain correction needs better inputs: the original station values instead of the grid (the table is rounded to 1 mGal), a 30 m DEM for the ground within 100 m of a station, and the density of the hills (the banded iron formation is 0.7 g/cc denser than the reduction density).
  • Depth still needs independent constraints (rock densities, boreholes, sections, seismic data), or the magnetic data of the same area: the joint inversion is the subject of a separate report.
